subject: Rio Grande
note: Cited to one pinned Wikipedia revision (trusted_secondary): Rio Grande. The page says the river is 3,051 km long and that the border stretch is 1,431 to 2,008 km 'depending on how the river is measured'; a script gives both ends and says so. It says the river marks the boundary 'since 1848' between El Paso and Ciudad Juarez and the Gulf, and that in 1899 a flood-control channel moved the river and created Cordova Island, the centre of the Chamizal dispute; the page does not say where on the river the Chamizal is, so the map puts no marker on it and draws no old river course (no sourced geometry). The 20% is the page's 'since the mid-twentieth century'. The Mexico-US border is not disputed; frames show only the river highlight and country outlines.

claims.text: The length of the Rio Grande is 1,896 miles (3,051 km), making it the fourth longest river in the United States and in North America by main stem; it originates in south-central Colorado and flows to the Gulf of Mexico.

After traversing the length of New Mexico, the Rio Grande becomes the Mexico–United States border, between the U.S. state of Texas and the northern Mexican states of Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas.
Since 1848, the Rio Grande has marked the boundary between Mexico and the United States from the twin cities of El Paso, Texas, and Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, to the Gulf of Mexico.
The segment of the river that forms the international border ranges from 889 to 1,248 miles (1,431 to 2,008 km), depending on how the river is measured.
During the late 1830s and early 1840s, the river marked the disputed border between Mexico and the nascent Republic of Texas; Mexico marked the border at the Nueces River.

In 1899, after a gradual change to the river position, a channel was dug for flood control which moved the river, creating what was called Cordova Island, which became the center of the Chamizal dispute.

Since the mid-twentieth century, only 20 percent of the Rio Grande's water reaches the Gulf of Mexico, because of the voluminous consumption of water required to irrigate farmland and to hydrate cities.

The United States and Mexico share the water of the river under a series of agreements administered by the International Boundary and Water Commission; the IBWC traces its roots to 1889, when the International Boundary Committee was established to maintain the border.
